name: Gutierrezia

project_scope.native_range_status: Gutierrezia texana target county certification unresolved

look_here_first: An annual open branching snakeweed might be G. texana, but A. amoena is almost identical at a glance. Turn the flower head sideways: look at individual phyllary NERVE borders, then compare the DISC floret's tiny pappus scales.

shared_traits: Small composite flower heads with ray and disc florets
Annual species and woody perennial subshrubs exist: avoid one silhouette for the whole genus

quick_key.if: Annual, open panicle; phyllary backs may show green nerve margins; tiny or absent disc pappus
Annual, open panicle with whiter uniform phyllary faces and visibly longer disc pappus
Annual, rounded flat-topped densely crowded flowering heads and longer disc pappus
Woody subshrub with dense terminal clusters each having about 3–8 rays
Woody subshrub, extremely tiny clusters of heads with only 1(–2) ray and disc floret

comparison_matrix.texana: Thin green nerve margin sometimes visible
FNA species 5–23; central Texas var. texana often 6–8

lookalike_cautions: Most important Central Texas double is G. texana versus Amphiachyris amoena. Neither branching nor yellow color alone works.
Amphiachyris dracunculoides has RADIATE heads. The stale discoid species wording was already corrected in its canonical card.
Do not treat unverified external snakeweed references as approved learner species.
Green phyllary nerve is frequently inconspicuous even in G. texana; use pappus/other traits too.

comparison_microlesson.title: Snakeweed or broomweed? Flip the tiny flower head.
steps: 1. Use whole plant habit just to shortlist: G. texana and A. amoena both have loose flowering arrays; A. dracunculoides often crowded.
2. Examine the underside of one flowering head: phyllaries are individual overlapping bracts below the yellow rays. Photograph the BACK not only front.

3. Look for thin green midnerve borders. G. texana MAY have a stripe or just dark green tips; A. amoena generally has uniformly pale whitish phyllary surfaces. Absence of stripe cannot conclusively rule out Gutierrezia.

4. For a stronger test, isolate one DISC floret from the center, NOT a marginal ray. Amphiachyris disc has a few long whitish narrowly spatulate pappus scales, often near the corolla length; Gutierrezia texana has a very short or nearly absent pappus.

5. If mature fruits remain, photograph G. texana short whitish crowns and contrast them against a separated Amphiachyris disc flower. Fruit photos cannot substitute for matched disc-floret photo in a measured dataset.

term_pronunciation.phyllary: FIL-uh-ree — one green bract under an Asteraceae flower head
term_pronunciation.pappus: PAP-us — hairs/scales/crown at the top of the cypsela or surrounding floret base
term_pronunciation.disc_floret: DISK FLOR-et — tiny central flower, not a yellow ray
term_pronunciation.cypsela: SIP-suh-luh — one-seeded dry fruit of a composite

comparison_microlesson.field_photo_instructions: Use macro or 10× lens, support stem, take front, side, back, mature fruit and whole branching shoot; include a real 1-mm ruler if possible. Avoid arrows that land in blank background or on ray florets when the term is a disc pappus.
